“Kisrā ibn Hurmuz. And wealth will become so abundant that a man will worry about finding someone willing to accept his money as charity.”

Earlier in this conversation, the Prophet had already confronted ʿAdī with two other points, but neither had moved him to accept Islam. When the subject of wealth came up in this way, however, ʿAdī later said:
“I have already seen two of these things, and by God, the third will certainly come.”
The text itself explains that by “the third” he meant the abundance of wealth.

The fact that wealth had acquired this level of importance in pre-Islamic society—an importance that could outweigh Bedouin customs and the respect traditionally given to those customs—could only become a broad social phenomenon in a society where purely Bedouin relations had already begun to lose their dominance.
At the same time, however, we should not look only at the signs of change. There were still many features of the older tribal system.

Nomadic migration remained common. Blood and descent still carried great weight. The whole tribe remained responsible for taking revenge on another tribe for one of its members who had been killed, even if the killing itself had been an individual act carried out for personal reasons.

The same applied to blood money. If a member of one tribe killed a member of another, the first tribe as a whole was still required to pay compensation to the other tribe as a whole, even when both the killing and its cause had been purely personal.
Migration also remained collective. The tribal chief decided when the tribe would move and where it would next settle.
The chief continued to lead the tribe in many matters of peace and in all matters of war, along with many other aspects of Bedouin life.

But these older forms now survived largely through the force of habit and continuity. Little by little, they were losing their economic foundations, and their place within the wider social structure was changing.

So far, we have looked broadly at the Arabian Peninsula during its final pre-Islamic period. But our subject now requires us to turn to the region that had a special historical importance at the time: the region where Arabia’s new historical development was taking shape.
This was what we call Western Arabia, where the Hijaz was located, and within the Hijaz, Mecca itself.
It was here, in particular, that the new history of Arabia was beginning to move.

It was also through this region that Arabia came into contact with the two great centers of the civilized world of the time: the Persian civilization to the east and the Byzantine civilization to the west.

The Hijaz, with Mecca at its center, stood at the meeting point of major international trade routes. These routes carried with them more than goods. They also brought other achievements of human history up to that time, at the beginning of the Middle Ages.

Together with these achievements, influences also entered the region from the countries ruled by, or dependent on, the two great empires. Persia and Byzantium were locked in a struggle over control of some of the most important parts of Asia and Africa surrounding the main sea routes, especially the Mediterranean and the Red Sea.
At that time, both empires represented, in their social systems, a historical mixture of two forms of society: slave society and feudal society.

The influences arriving from abroad through the trade routes—together with social, political, cultural and religious influences—interacted actively with the forces of change already developing inside Arab society during the final pre-Islamic period.
It was through this interaction that the new history of Arabia began to take shape.

In this region, at this particular time, we can see a historical process unfolding. Its signs appeared one after another, often overlapping, across economic, social, political, cultural and religious life.
The features we have already examined as signs of the breakdown of primitive tribal society represented only one side of this process: the side of destruction.
We must now look at the other side as well—the side of formation and birth.
A study of the historical conditions of this period allows us to identify the forces driving Arabia in a new historical direction.
We will begin that study with Mecca.

One of the more curious explanations given by Arab chroniclers for the name Mecca is that it comes from the verb imtakka, used of a young camel when it sucks all the milk from its mother’s udder and leaves nothing behind.
From this supposed origin, they explained the name by saying that Mecca “draws people in” or “sucks them toward itself” because it is a sacred city.

Classical lexicographers adopted similar explanations. They said that makka or imtakka could mean to suck something completely dry, or to diminish it, and that the sacred city was called Mecca because “it diminishes sins, removes them, or destroys anyone who commits injustice there.”
This kind of explanation is subjective and has no real historical value. Even so, it reflects the special place Mecca held in Arab history before Islam.

Its past was considered ancient, and the chroniclers told many stories about its earliest period. As one scholar puts it, “the chroniclers undoubtedly created stories of this kind because they believed such stories would make the sacred city appear more ancient and would present it as the sanctuary of all the Arabs before Islam.”
Several centuries before the Arab chroniclers, Ptolemy referred in his Geography to a place called Mocaraba, which has been identified with Mecca. He may have been expressing something similar.
Jawād ʿAlī interprets the word Mocaraba as something like muqarraba, from the idea of drawing near, because Mecca was “a sacred city in which people drew near to the idols with offerings.”
The name used by Ptolemy does not appear in the works of other classical geographers and historians, apart from later Arab chroniclers.

Even so, this reference by an ancient geographer—one whose work was later relied on by Arab geographers of the Middle Ages—is extremely useful. It gives us evidence that Mecca was known in Ptolemy’s time, in the second century AD.
Before that period, however, we lack reliable evidence that can shed much light on its history.
All these attempts to explain the name “Mecca” point to one thing: even in its earlier history, the city held a distinctive position in Arabia.
Whether that position originally came from religious importance or from other historical causes, Mecca clearly occupied a central place in the history of the pre-Islamic period that concerns us here.
Our subject is the beginning of a major historical shift: the transformation of the structures on which the old pre-Islamic order rested.

The period that matters most to us is therefore the period in which the signs of this change become visible. It is also the period that is least obscure to the historian, compared with earlier times for which reliable evidence remains scarce.

According to the Arab chroniclers, Quraysh first gained leadership over Mecca under Quṣayy ibn Kilāb. Before him, leadership had belonged to Khuzāʿa. Quṣayy took it from them during the time of ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥārith, known as Abū Ghubshān al-Khuzāʿī.

The accounts differ over exactly how Quṣayy gained control, but they agree that it did not happen without conflict. Fighting took place, and Quṣayy eventually defeated Khuzāʿa, either directly in war or after the dispute was referred for judgment to Yaʿmur ibn ʿAwf ibn Kaʿb of Kināna.
We do not know the exact date of these events.

The chroniclers give us little help except for one clue in a report claiming that Quṣayy bought control of the Kaʿba from Abū Ghubshān al-Khuzāʿī in exchange for a wineskin and a camel. This transaction was said to have given rise to the proverb:
“A worse bargain than the bargain of Abū Ghubshān.”
The same report says that this happened during the reign of al-Mundhir ibn al-Nuʿmān, king of al-Ḥīra.
Even though this detail appears within the legendary story of the “bargain,” it gives us an indirect clue about when Quraysh, represented by Quṣayy, first gained leadership over Mecca.
The al-Mundhir ibn al-Nuʿmān mentioned here must be the son of al-Nuʿmān I ibn Imruʾ al-Qays II.

It cannot be the later al-Mundhir ibn al-Nuʿmān of 631–632, “whom the Arabs called al-Gharūr and who was killed in Bahrain on the day of Jawāthā,” and who ruled al-Ḥīra for only eight months, “until Khālid ibn al-Walīd arrived in al-Ḥīra.” That ruler belonged to the period when Islam had already appeared.
The earlier al-Mundhir succeeded his father al-Nuʿmān I as ruler of al-Ḥīra in AD 418.
From this indirect evidence, we can conclude that Quraysh gained leadership over Mecca during the first half of the fifth century.
In our view, this conclusion is probably correct. It also gives the events and developments of late pre-Islamic Western Arabia a normal historical logic.

The changes associated with the period of Quraysh’s rule in Mecca could hardly have arisen during the very short period immediately before the appearance of Islam, as the reports of the chroniclers might sometimes suggest.
Historical development requires more time than that.

For the same reason, the role played by Quṣayy himself at the beginning of Quraysh’s leadership in Mecca should not really be seen as the beginning of the process. It was more likely the result of a much longer historical development in which Mecca had already played an important role.

The developments that appeared once Quraysh’s leadership was firmly established under Quṣayy represented a qualitative leap—a major change produced by many smaller changes that had already been building over time.
These earlier changes grew out of an increasingly close relationship between two developments.
On one side was the new division of labor taking shape both in settled communities and in the desert.
On the other was the expansion of commercial middlemen and the growing use of money in exchange across the markets of the Arabian Peninsula.
The chroniclers agree that once Quṣayy had secured leadership over Mecca, a number of major changes followed.

They give us many complicated and sometimes inconsistent details. But beneath those details lies historical material that helps us understand both the changes themselves and the direction in which they were moving.
Once we separate the useful evidence from the surrounding details, several main points emerge.
The chroniclers say that when Quṣayy took control of Quraysh in Mecca, he divided Mecca into residential quarters among his people and assigned each group of Quraysh its place.
We do not need to accept the chroniclers’ suggestion that Quṣayy simply decided, by his own personal will, to reorganize the city in this way.
What matters to us is the historical meaning of the event.

We see it as the result of objective historical conditions rather than the decision of one individual. A particular process of development had matured to the point where this change became possible at the right time and in the right place.
To understand its historical meaning, however, we first have to understand what the change actually involved.
In practice, it amounted to a social classification of the inhabitants of Mecca from among the clans of Quraysh and their allies.
One group occupied the central parts of Mecca around the Kaʿba. Because they lived in the biṭāḥ, the low-lying central area, they became known as Quraysh al-Biṭāḥ.
A second, lower-ranking group lived on the outskirts of Mecca and became known as Quraysh al-Ẓawāhir.
But what was this classification based on?
We know that Quraysh al-Ẓawāhir were poor or only partly settled, and that their financial position was weak. Quraysh al-Biṭāḥ, by contrast, included “the merchants and the wealthy.”
So the division was based on financial, economic and social position rather than on tribal custom.
Both groups belonged either to Quraysh itself or to groups allied with Quraysh. One was Quraysh al-Biṭāḥ and the other Quraysh al-Ẓawāhir. Both, in that sense, were part of Quraysh.

If tribal belonging alone had determined the division, all the clans of Quraysh would have occupied the preferred central area, while the allied clans from outside Quraysh would have been placed on the outskirts.
But that was no longer how things worked.
The old tribal values had already begun to weaken, together with the tribal system itself.
A new situation was producing new values. Commercial and social development was placing financial and trading position above older tribal considerations.
This is why Banū ʿAbd Manāf and Banū ʿAbd al-Dār came to stand at the front of Quraysh al-Biṭāḥ: they had become wealthier and more powerful in trade.

The same standard continued to operate afterward. The Umayyads eventually took the leading position within pre-Islamic Quraysh because they became its richest merchants and extended their financial influence over many tribes of the Hijaz outside Mecca.

If we go back to the beginning of Quraysh’s leadership—that is, to the period of Quṣayy, which the chroniclers treat as its starting point—we find that Ibn al-Kalbī and Ibn Isḥāq give essentially the same explanation for the transfer of power in Mecca from Khuzāʿa to Quraysh.
They say that when Ḥulayl ibn Ḥubshiyya, chief of Khuzāʿa and father of Ḥubbā, Quṣayy’s wife, died, Abū Ghubshān took over the guardianship of the Kaʿba.

By this time, however, “the descendants of Quṣayy had spread, his wealth had increased, and his standing had grown. Quṣayy therefore believed that he had a stronger claim than Khuzāʿa and Banū Bakr to the Kaʿba and to authority over Mecca.”

Here, even within the traditional account, we can see that the growth of wealth—and the higher social standing that came with it—was treated as a legitimate basis for Quṣayy’s claim to rule over the Kaʿba and Mecca.
